```{r setup, include=FALSE}

  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 10,
  fig.height = 8
)

# install.packages("skimr")
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)
library(emmeans)
# library(skimr)
```



```{r load-data}

housing_raw <- read_csv(
  params$data_file,
  col_types = cols(
    id = col_character(),
    date = col_character(),
    zipcode = col_character(),
    .default = col_guess()
  ),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

sale_dates <- as.Date(substr(housing_raw$date, 1, 8), format = "%Y%m%d")
```


```{r raw_data_overview}
raw_overview <- tibble(
  Metric = c(
    "Number of sale records",
    "Number of columns",
    "Unique property IDs",
    "Rows beyond first occurrence of a property ID",
    "Earliest sale date",
    "Latest sale date"
  ),
  Value = c(
    format(nrow(housing_raw), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
    ncol(housing_raw),
    format(n_distinct(housing_raw$id), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
    sum(duplicated(housing_raw$id)),
    as.character(min(sale_dates, na.rm = TRUE)),
    as.character(max(sale_dates, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
)

kable(raw_overview, caption = "Raw dataset overview")
```



```{r filter_dates_NO_LONGER}
# Filter Sale Dates
# 
# The initial portion of the dataset is excluded to restrict the analysis to a complete 12-month period (May 28, 2014, to May 27, 2015) and avoid overrepresenting seasonal patterns in housing sales.


housing_filtered <- housing_raw %>%
  mutate(sale_date = sale_dates)%>%
  filter(
    between(sale_date, as.Date("2014-05-28"), as.Date("2015-05-27"))
  )

filtered_overview <- tibble(
  Metric = c(
    "Number of sale records",
    "Number of columns",
    "Unique property IDs",
    "Rows beyond first occurrence of a property ID",
    "Earliest sale date",
    "Latest sale date"
  ),
  Value = c(
    format(nrow(housing_filtered), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
    ncol(housing_filtered),
    format(n_distinct(housing_filtered$id), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
    sum(duplicated(housing_filtered$id)),
    as.character(min(housing_filtered$sale_date, na.rm = TRUE)),
    as.character(max(housing_filtered$sale_date, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
)

kable(filtered_overview, caption = "Filtered dataset overview")
```


```{r create_age_renovation_variables}
housing_filtered <- housing_filtered %>%
  mutate(
    sale_year = as.integer(format(sale_date, "%Y")),
    age = sale_year - yr_built,
    renovated = if_else(yr_renovated > 0, 1L, 0L),
    age_since_renovation = if_else(
      renovated == 1,
      sale_year - yr_renovated,
      0
    )
  )
```



```{r data_summary_1}
glimpse(housing_filtered)
```


```{r data_summary_2}
summary(housing_filtered)
```


```{r filter_out_negative_ages}
negative_age_overview <- tibble(
  Metric = c(
    "Records with negative age",
    "Records with negative age since renovation",
    "Total records with either negative age"
  ),
  Count = c(
    sum(housing_filtered$age < 0),
    sum(housing_filtered$age_since_renovation < 0),
    sum(
      housing_filtered$age < 0 |
      housing_filtered$age_since_renovation < 0
    )
  )
)

kable(negative_age_overview, caption = "Invalid property and renovation ages")

# Remove records with negative ages
housing_filtered <- housing_filtered %>%
  filter(
    age >= 0,
    age_since_renovation >= 0
  )
```



```{r raw-missingness}
missing_summary <- tibble(
  Variable = names(housing_filtered),
  Missing = vapply(housing_filtered, function(x) sum(is.na(x)), integer(1))
) %>%
  mutate(`Missing (%)` = round(100 * Missing / nrow(housing_raw), 2))

kable(missing_summary, caption = "Missing values in the raw data")
```




## 2. Duplicate house IDs and latest-sale selection

The same `id` can appear multiple times because a house was sold more than once in the observation period. First, count **distinct house IDs with more than one sale record** (not just the number of surplus rows). Then keep the record with the **latest sale date** for each house. This step happens **before** the exploration–confirmation split.

If two rows for a house share the same latest sale date, the first occurrence in the original CSV is retained as a reproducible tie-breaker. An unparseable sale date stops the analysis rather than silently selecting an arbitrary record.

```{r duplicate_ids_latest_sale}
housing_dated <- housing_filtered %>%
  mutate(
    sale_date = as.Date(substr(date, 1, 8), format = "%Y%m%d"),
    original_row = row_number()
  )

if (anyNA(housing_dated$sale_date)) {
  stop("Some sale dates could not be parsed; review the raw data before filtering.")
}

id_sale_counts <- housing_dated %>%
  count(id, name = "Sale_records")

repeated_ids <- id_sale_counts %>%
  filter(Sale_records > 1)

housing_latest <- housing_dated %>%
  arrange(id, desc(sale_date), original_row) %>%
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(-sale_date, -original_row)

stopifnot(
  nrow(housing_latest) == n_distinct(housing_filtered$id),
  anyDuplicated(housing_latest$id) == 0
)

duplicate_summary <- tibble(
  Metric = c(
    "Raw sale records",
    "Unique house IDs",
    "House IDs appearing more than once",
    "Extra sale records from repeated house IDs",
    "Records retained (latest sale per house)"
  ),
  Count = c(
    nrow(housing_filtered),
    n_distinct(housing_filtered$id),
    nrow(repeated_ids),
    sum(repeated_ids$Sale_records - 1),
    nrow(housing_latest)
  )
)

kable(
  duplicate_summary,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  caption = "Repeated-house audit and latest-sale filtering"
)
```


## 3. Allocate 30% to exploration and 70% to confirmation

We now split **`housing_latest`**, which has exactly one latest-sale row per house. A fixed random seed makes this allocation reproducible. All subsequent descriptive statistics, plots, and correlations use the exploration sample only.

```{r split_data}
set.seed(params$random_seed)

property_ids <- housing_latest$id
exploration_ids <- sample(
  property_ids,
  size = round(0.30 * length(property_ids)),
  replace = FALSE
)

housing_exploration <- housing_latest %>%
  filter(id %in% exploration_ids)

housing_confirmation <- housing_latest %>%
  filter(!id %in% exploration_ids)

stopifnot(
  nrow(housing_exploration) + nrow(housing_confirmation) == nrow(housing_latest),
  length(intersect(housing_exploration$id, housing_confirmation$id)) == 0,
  anyDuplicated(housing_exploration$id) == 0,
  anyDuplicated(housing_confirmation$id) == 0
)

split_summary <- tibble(
  Sample = c("Exploration", "Confirmation", "Total"),
  `Sale records` = c(
    nrow(housing_exploration),
    nrow(housing_confirmation),
    nrow(housing_latest)
  ),
  `Percent of records` = c(
    100 * nrow(housing_exploration) / nrow(housing_latest),
    100 * nrow(housing_confirmation) / nrow(housing_latest),
    100
  ),
  `Unique properties` = c(
    n_distinct(housing_exploration$id),
    n_distinct(housing_confirmation$id),
    n_distinct(housing_latest$id)
  )
) %>%
  mutate(`Percent of records` = round(`Percent of records`, 2))

kable(split_summary, caption = "Exploration/confirmation allocation (latest sale per house)")
```


## 4. Exploratory descriptive statistics


```{r exploratory_descriptives}
numeric_variables <- names(housing_exploration)[
  vapply(housing_exploration, is.numeric, logical(1))
]

numeric_variables <- setdiff(numeric_variables, c("id", "zipcode"))

numeric_summary <- bind_rows(lapply(numeric_variables, function(variable) {
  x <- housing_exploration[[variable]]
  tibble(
    Variable = variable,
    N = sum(!is.na(x)),
    Mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    P0 = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    P25 = unname(quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)),
    P50 = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    P75 = unname(quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)),
    P100 = max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}))

kable(
  numeric_summary,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
  caption = "Numeric summaries for the 30% exploration sample"
)
```

Note that `waterfront` is binary and `view`, `condition`, and `grade` use ordered codes. Their numerical summaries may be useful for an audit, but distributions by category are generally easier to interpret than their means.

## 5. Univariate distributions

### Histograms of key quantitative variables

```{r univariate_histograms, fig.width=11, fig.height=10}
histogram_variables <- c(
  "price", "sqft_living", "sqft_lot",
  "age", "age_since_renovation"
)

histogram_data <- housing_exploration %>%
  mutate(
    age_since_renovation = if_else(
      renovated == 1, age_since_renovation, NA_real_
    )
  ) %>%
  select(all_of(histogram_variables)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Value",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) %>%
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = histogram_variables))

ggplot(histogram_data, aes(x = Value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = "#4472A5", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Distributions of key housing variables",
    subtitle = "30% exploration sample; renovation age includes only renovated properties",
    x = "Value (units vary by panel)",
    y = "Number of sales"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```


```{r price-distribution, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
ggplot(housing_exploration, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 35,
    fill = "#4472A5",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(

    y = "Number of sales"

  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +

```

### Log-scale views of right-skewed variables

A small number of expensive houses or very large lots can visually compress most observations in a standard histogram. For strictly positive observations, log10 scaling makes the shape of the distribution easier to see. These plots **do not remove or modify observations used in later analyses**.

```{r univariate_log_histograms, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
log_variables <- c("price", "sqft_living", "sqft_lot")

log_histogram_data <- housing_exploration %>%
  select(all_of(log_variables)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Value), Value > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    LogValue = log(Value),
    Variable = factor(Variable, levels = log_variables)
  )

ggplot(log_histogram_data, aes(x = LogValue)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = "#527F6D", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Natural log-transformed distributions",
    subtitle = "30% exploration sample",
    x = "ln(value)",
    y = "Number of sales"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

### Frequency distributions of discrete and categorical variables

```{r univariate-bar-charts, fig.width=11, fig.height=10}
bar_variables <- c(

  "view", "condition", "grade", "renovated"
)

bar_data <- housing_exploration %>%
  select(all_of(bar_variables)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),

ggplot(bar_data, aes(x = Value)) +
```

```{r grade-frequency}
grade_frequency <- housing_exploration %>%
  count(grade, name = "Count") %>%
  complete(grade = 1:13, fill = list(Count = 0)) %>%
  mutate(Percentage = 100 * Count / sum(Count)) %>%
  arrange(grade)

kable(
  grade_frequency,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Frequency distribution of construction grades"
)
```


```{r group-housing-grades}
housing_exploration <- housing_exploration %>%
  mutate(
    grade_ = factor(
      case_when(
        grade <= 5 ~ "1-5",
        grade >= 12 ~ "12-13",
        TRUE ~ as.character(grade)
      ),
      levels = c("7", "1-5", "6", as.character(8:11), "12-13")
    )
  )

grade_group_frequency <- housing_exploration %>%
  count(grade_, name = "Count") %>%
  mutate(Percentage = 100 * Count / sum(Count)) %>%
  arrange(as.numeric(sub("-.*", "", as.character(grade_))))

kable(
  grade_group_frequency,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Frequency distribution of grouped construction grades"
)
```


## 6. Bivariate associations with sale price (exploration sample)

### Scatterplots: sale price versus quantitative characteristics

We focus on living area, lot area, surrounding-home living area, and construction year. The horizontal axis uses its own scale in each panel; the vertical axis is consistently sale price in dollars.

```{r bivariate-scatterplots, fig.width=11, fig.height=9}
scatter_variables <- c(
  "sqft_living", "sqft_lot", "age", "age_since_renovation"
)

scatter_data <- housing_exploration %>%
  mutate(
    age_since_renovation = if_else(
      renovated == 1, age_since_renovation, NA_real_
    )
  ) %>%
  select(price, all_of(scatter_variables)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(scatter_variables),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(price), !is.na(Value)) %>%
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = scatter_variables))

ggplot(scatter_data, aes(x = Value, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.16, size = 0.7, color = "#38658D") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8, color = "#C05A46") +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) {
    paste0("$", format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE))
  }) +
  labs(
    title = "Housing characteristics and sale price",
    subtitle = "30% exploration sample; renovation age includes only renovated properties",
    x = "Characteristic value (units vary by panel)",
    y = "Sale price (USD)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```

### Closer look: living area versus sale price on log scales

This alternative view can reveal patterns that are difficult to see when very large houses and high-price sales dominate the original axes. **Neither the log-scale relationship nor the fitted line is a causal estimate.**

```{r bivariate-log-scatter, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}
log_scatter_data <- housing_exploration %>%
  filter(!is.na(price), !is.na(sqft_living),
         price > 0, sqft_living > 0)

ggplot(log_scatter_data, aes(x = sqft_living, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.20, size = 0.8, color = "#38658D") +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
    aes(color = "OLS"),
    se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess", formula = y ~ x,
    aes(color = "LOESS"),
    se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Trend line",
    values = c("OLS" = "#C05A46", "LOESS" = "#4472A5"),
    breaks = c("OLS", "LOESS")
  ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10(labels = function(x) {
    paste0("$", format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE))
  }) +
  labs(
    title = "Living area and sale price (log–log axes)",
    subtitle = "Exploration sample; unadjusted linear and nonlinear associations",
    x = "Living area (sq. ft., log scale)",
    y = "Sale price (USD, log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

### Sale-price distributions across coded property characteristics

For discrete characteristics such as waterfront status, view quality, and construction grade, boxplots communicate group differences more clearly than scatterplots. The log10 sale-price axis improves readability across the wide range of recorded prices.

```{r bivariate-boxplots, fig.width=10, fig.height=15}
group_variables <- c(
  "grade", "waterfront", "view", "condition", "renovated"
)

price_by_group <- housing_exploration %>%
  select(price, all_of(group_variables)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(group_variables),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Level"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(price), price > 0, !is.na(Level)) %>%
  mutate(
    Level = factor(Level, levels = sort(unique(Level))),
    Variable = factor(Variable, levels = group_variables)
  )

ggplot(price_by_group, aes(x = Level, y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "#A9C7D8", color = "#385C77",
    outlier.alpha = 0.18
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = function(x) {
    paste0("$", format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE))
  }) +
  labs(
    title = "Sale-price distributions by property characteristics",
    subtitle = "30% exploration sample; boxplots on a logarithmic price axis",
    x = "Category code",
    y = "Sale price (USD, log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")
```

**Interpretation reminder:** Scatterplots and group comparisons show marginal patterns. A later descriptive multiple regression can summarize *adjusted associations*, but it does not by itself make those associations causal.

## 7. Exploratory correlation matrix

The matrix below uses selected quantitative variables from the **30% exploration sample**, including sale price. We intentionally exclude `id` and `zipcode` (identifiers), `lat` and `long` (coordinates), and the coded categorical/ordinal variables (`waterfront`, `view`, `condition`, `grade`). We also exclude `yr_renovated`, whose value of zero indicates no recorded renovation rather than a literal year.

**Important:** Pearson correlations describe *unadjusted linear associations*. They are not regression coefficients, do not account for ZIP-code fixed effects, and do not establish causality.

```{r correlation-matrix}
correlation_variables <- c(
  "price",
  "bedrooms",
  "bathrooms",
  "sqft_living",
  "sqft_lot",
  "floors",
  "sqft_above",
  "sqft_basement",
  "yr_built",
  "sqft_living15",
  "sqft_lot15"
)

correlation_data <- housing_exploration %>%
  select(all_of(correlation_variables))

correlation_matrix <- cor(
  correlation_data,
  method = "pearson",
  use = "complete.obs"
)

kable(
  round(correlation_matrix, 2),
  caption = "Pearson correlation matrix: exploration sample"
)
```

### Correlation heatmap

```{r correlation-heatmap-spearman, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
correlation_variables_spearman <- c(
  "price", "grade", "sqft_living",
  "sqft_lot", "age",
  "condition", "renovated"
)

correlation_matrix_spearman <- housing_exploration %>%
  select(all_of(correlation_variables_spearman)) %>%
  cor(method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")

correlations_long_spearman <- as.data.frame(as.table(correlation_matrix_spearman)) %>%
  rename(Variable_1 = Var1, Variable_2 = Var2, Correlation = Freq) %>%
  mutate(
    Variable_1 = factor(Variable_1, levels = rev(correlation_variables_spearman)),
    Variable_2 = factor(Variable_2, levels = correlation_variables_spearman)
  )

ggplot(correlations_long_spearman, aes(x = Variable_2, y = Variable_1, fill = Correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Correlation)), size = 2.7) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B35806",
    midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Correlations among key housing variables",
    subtitle = "Spearman rank correlation",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Spearman \u03C1"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 50, hjust = 1),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )
```

### Variables most correlated with sale price

```{r correlations-with-price}
price_correlations <- tibble(
  Variable = rownames(correlation_matrix_spearman),
  Spearman = as.numeric(correlation_matrix_spearman[, "price"]),

  filter(Variable != "price") %>%
```

## 8. Modeling

```{r model_2-living-area}
model_2 <- lm(
  log(price) ~ log(sqft_living),
  data = housing_exploration
)

coeftest(model_2, vcov. = vcovHC(model_2))
cat("R-squared:", round(summary(model_2)$r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(model_2)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")
cat("Observations:", nobs(model_2), "\n")
```



```{r model-2-plot-preparation}
loess_data <- housing_exploration %>%
  mutate(
    log_price = log(price),
    log_sqft_living = log(sqft_living)
  )

loess_model_2 <- loess(
  log_price ~ log_sqft_living,
  data = loess_data,
  span = 0.75
)

# Create prediction dataframe
model_2_plot_data <- tibble(
  log_sqft_living = seq(
    min(loess_data$log_sqft_living),
    max(loess_data$log_sqft_living),
    length.out = 500
  )
)

# Create living area variable
model_2_plot_data$sqft_living <- exp(
  model_2_plot_data$log_sqft_living
)

# Generate OLS predictions
model_2_plot_data$OLS <- predict(
  model_2,
  newdata = model_2_plot_data
)

# Generate LOESS predictions
model_2_plot_data$LOESS <- predict(
  loess_model_2,
  newdata = model_2_plot_data
)

# Reshape for plotting
model_2_plot_data <- model_2_plot_data %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(OLS, LOESS),
    names_to = "Model",
    values_to = "estimated_log_price"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    estimated_price = exp(estimated_log_price)
  )
```


```{r model-2-loess-log-log, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = loess_data,
    aes(x = log_sqft_living, y = log_price),
    alpha = 0.15,
    size = 0.8,
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = model_2_plot_data,
    aes(
      x = log_sqft_living,
      y = estimated_log_price,
      color = Model
    ),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("OLS" = "#C05A46", "LOESS" = "#4472A5"),
    breaks = c("OLS", "LOESS")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Log Living Area and Log Sale Price",
    subtitle = "Comparison of OLS and LOESS fits",
    x = "Log of Living Area",
    y = "Log of Sale Price",
    color = "Trend Line"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r complete-model-predicted-actual-log, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}

    actual_price = exp(actual_log_price),
    predicted_price = exp(predicted_log_price)

ggplot(

  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted vs. Actual Log Sale Prices",

    y = "Predicted Log Sale Price",

  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
```
